title: Resurrecting the Champ
full_review:
In director Rod Lurie's compelling film "Resurrecting the Champ" (Yari Film Group), the evolving friendship between young sportswriter Erik Kernan (Josh Hartnett) and a homeless former boxer who calls himself "Champ" (Samuel L. Jackson) leads to a series of unexpected revelations.

In the course of the film, based on true events, Erik is forced to take a fresh look at himself and to re-evaluate his basic relationships, including those with his wife, Joyce (Kathryn Morris), his son, Teddy (Dakota Goyo), and the troubling memory of his deceased father. He is haunted by the professional renown and personal shortcomings of his late father, a famous boxing announcer.

Erik and Champ first encounter each other when the younger man plays the role of good Samaritan, rescuing Champ from a group of teenage bullies who are mocking and beating him. Erik only really becomes interested in his new acquaintance, however, when he learns of the homeless man's past glory. Here at last, it seems, is the "big story" Erik has been waiting for, the one that will demonstrate to his editor, Metz (Alan Alda), that he can deliver the goods. But he plans to do so by giving the story to another editor at the paper.

Such a breakthrough is important to him personally as well. Although separated from his wife (a "hard news" reporter with a reputation superior to his), Erik is determined to win her back and to be reunited with his son.

When his article about Champ is published, he indeed becomes the man of the hour, celebrated by his newspaper, wooed by others and pursued by television casting agent Andrea Flak (Teri Hatcher). When unexpected circumstances undermine his plan, Erik must make a series of difficult choices that will define who he is far more profoundly than his brief career as a celebrity.

This is a deeply moving -- and moral -- film. With the possible exception of Joyce, who serves as her husband's unswerving moral compass, all the other central characters are morally complex, and all the more interesting for it. But, for all their shortcomings, none of them proves to be beyond redemption.

An excellent script is matched by three outstanding performances. Jackson's Champ is irrepressibly optimistic, but also shrewd and careful of his dignity. Hartnett, as Erik, pays attention to the details, including his character's initial reluctance to have any physical contact with Champ. And Peter Coyote, as seedy boxing manager Epstein, turns a cameo into a showstopper.

Director Rod Lurie shows particular flair for the boxing sequences, utilizing lurid colors and speed in sharp contrast to Martin Scorsese's "Raging Bull" with its celebrated black-and-white, slow-motion techniques, although they may prove disturbing to those with a low tolerance for the sport.

The film contains occasional vulgarity and profanity, boxing violence including one sequence with blood, skimpy costuming and suggestive movements, public urination and images of a disturbing body scar. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults (though it's probably acceptable for most older teens). The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
